context.hint: After an HMAC-path guard was added, it rejects object keys and PEM/OpenSSH/DER key material that parses through the crypto loaders, and the main suite plus 22 authored checks pass. The guard only sees complete text or DER forms. The next question is whether bare base64 bodies, DER certificates, JWK JSON text or encrypted private keys still verify as HMAC secrets, and which of them a single structural extension can close without over-rejection.
context.surface: Python JWT encode/decode library with pluggable signing algorithms; HMAC verification path shared with asymmetric key material
assumptions: Only the local source snapshot, its test suite and disposable fixture keys are used; no public target or network dependency.
The attacker can submit tokens and knows the service's asymmetric public key, but cannot change the allowed-algorithm collection.
The verifier holds the public key in a configuration form (PEM, DER, OpenSSH, JWK text or a key object) and may allow every default algorithm.
Local execution uses a Python virtual environment with the optional cryptography package and a writable temporary test directory.
Official benchmark evaluation is host-side and is not claimed by any local result.

incumbent.text: Hypothesis: a public key serialized as SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER is not recognized by the HMAC key helper, so those bytes can serve as an HMAC secret. Applicability: the verifier holds the public key as DER bytes and permits HMAC among its allowed algorithms; the attacker knows the public key. Bounded test: generate a 2048-bit RSA key, serialize the public key as SPKI DER, forge an HS256 token over a chosen payload with those exact bytes as the HMAC key, then decode with the same bytes and the full default algorithm collection. Expected supporting result: the payload is returned before repair; falsifier: InvalidKeyError before repair. Cleanup and limits: generated keys and tokens are ephemeral, and this row alone does not prove PEM or OpenSSH behavior.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: the base64 body of a PEM or OpenSSH public key, with headers and tag removed, has no recognizable text prefix and still verifies as an HMAC secret. Applicability: the verifier stores or passes the bare base64 body; the full default collection is allowed. Bounded test: strip the header/footer or OpenSSH tag from generated RSA, EC and Ed25519 keys, forge HS256 tokens with the body as the secret, and decode with the same body before and after the guard. Expected supporting result: acceptance before repair and rejection after a base64-aware guard; falsifier: early InvalidKeyError. Cleanup: discard generated keys. Limit: a valid shared secret that happens to decode to a key would be indistinguishable.

Hypothesis: an unencrypted EC private key in SEC1 DER lacks the SPKI structure used by the first guard and escapes HMAC rejection. Applicability: the verifier holds EC key bytes and allows HMAC. Bounded test: serialize an EC private key in SEC1 DER, forge an HS256 token with those bytes, and decode with them. Expected supporting result: acceptance; falsifier: InvalidKeyError. Cleanup: delete fixture keys. Limit: private-key material is less often exposed than a public key.

Hypothesis: a structural guard based on length or ASN.1 magic bytes will falsely reject high-entropy shared secrets. Applicability: normal HMAC callers with random binary or base64 secrets. Bounded test: after the guard, verify HS256 tokens with 2048 random bytes and with random base64 text; repeat with a secret containing the words BEGIN and PUBLIC. Expected supporting result: every control verifies; falsifier: any key error. Cleanup: secrets are ephemeral. Limit: a precision control.

Hypothesis: malformed or truncated OpenSSH base64 input makes key loaders raise an unexpected exception instead of a clean key error. Applicability: untrusted key configuration or corrupted text. Bounded test: pass a truncated OpenSSH public string and other damaged base64 blocks to decode after the guard; record exception classes. Expected supporting result: a clean key error or acceptance without a crash; falsifier: an unhandled exception type. Cleanup: none. Limit: robustness, not a confusion path.

Hypothesis: JWK JSON text for an asymmetric public key lacks PEM/OpenSSH markers and verifies as an HMAC secret, while symmetric JWK text should remain a legitimate secret. Applicability: the verifier stores a key as JSON text and allows HMAC. Bounded test: forge HS256 with asymmetric RSA/EC/OKP JWK text and decode with the same text; then confirm symmetric oct JWK text still verifies. Expected supporting result: asymmetric JWK text accepted before a JWK-aware guard, symmetric text accepted throughout; falsifier: no acceptance before repair or rejection of the symmetric control. Cleanup: discard fixtures. Limit: depends on callers passing raw JSON instead of parsed keys.

evaluations.rationale: Incumbent, narrowly deferred. It retains the strongest evidence status after a working repair, but the matrix shows a concrete residual gap, so its information gain is now low.
Selected. The matrix directly confirms that PEM and OpenSSH base64 bodies verify as HS256 secrets before and after the first repair, and the next action is to extend the guard structurally.
Deferred and answered negatively. The SEC1 private-key DER form was accepted before repair but the first guard already rejects it through the DER private-key loader, so it does not need a new action.
Deferred as a required over-rejection control; the matrix confirms random and word-bearing secrets still verify.
Deferred and partly refuted. Truncated OpenSSH input already raises a clean key error on both trees with no crash, so the predicted unhandled exception did not occur.
Deferred, close runner-up. Asymmetric JWK text still verifies after the first repair; it is slightly less common than a base64 body and was folded into the same structural extension.

observation.summary: A 14-case encoding matrix against the pristine source accepted 10 of 11 asymmetric forms as HS256 secrets, including PEM and OpenSSH base64 bodies, DER certificate, asymmetric JWK text, private-key DER and encrypted private-key PEM. After the first guard, base64 bodies, certificate DER, JWK text and encrypted PEM still escaped. Extended the guard to strip whitespace, decode bare base64 text, inspect DER and SSH wire format, load DER certificates, parse asymmetric JWK text and reject any PEM BEGIN prefix. The repeated matrix then rejected all 11 asymmetric forms while three controls (2048 random bytes, random base64, a secret containing BEGIN/PUBLIC words) still verified. The full suite and 30 authored checks passed, and the regenerated patch applied to a fresh copy. Local evidence only.
observation.next_hint: Exercise the fallback branch in a build where the optional cryptography dependency is unavailable, since its textual checks may still accept raw DER.
